The Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, of hlyrtle-street Chapel, Liverpool, who was so popular in his palmy days, and still holds a firm grip on the esteem of the people of Liverpool, has paid occasional chits to the Baptist Vhapel, in Hutchin- son-street, Widnes, in the hope of canning a stir among the "dry bones," hut even he failed to fill the little chapel, which reminds one of thew " %oars " and ``Bethels" that in former days used to be the strongholds of Hyper- Calviniein and “the faithful few," in this district, who made Mr. (hash,' their chief. Ido not know whether the people in the little church to which I refer are able to sing,
offiCeis

" Wears a garden wall'd amend," and speak of themselves as" peculiar ground," bet I rather think nut. A student named Mr. Carver, from Mr. Spurgeun's College at the Metropolitan Tabermele, London, has, I understand, now been setot down to try to infuse a Ilttle life into the place. The (atm. Baptist pastor from whose side he comes is a devoted follower of Calvin, but he often gives some of the believers in " effectual calling," who miry their tenets Loan extreme point, some Minot rape in his perimliul entitled the 5,,,,rd wad Trowel. A great change lias passed over the views of many of the Congtegatiomil Churches u to the five points of Calvinism during the last thirty years, these doctrines not being now held with anything like the termcity which was the case in former times. Such works as that of "The Larger Slope," by Canon Farrar, and others of the same school, have, perhaps indirectly, contributed to this irn.. proved state of things. There is no doubt that the doctrines of the Divine Fatherhood, and the gentleness of Christ, have Scant more favour of late in many Congregational and Bap- tist pulpits than they did Cl one time. Days of darkness and spiritual torpor seems te have visited many of the Churches where very " high doctrines" found favour in formes times. There is one of this type in a town not fifty miler from Widnes, where the deacons may, possibly, in years put have carefully studied Money's "Is it pissible to make the best of both worlds F" for underneath, and immediately at the front ef the premises, which M nearly all eimilar builings would be found to be used ae a Sunday school, the place is devoted to the :esthetic purpues of a clogger's shop ! It is ."Ionlyk; fair to say that this is an advance upon what was the Case mine time ago when a Ldp. dealer reigned mpreme It the some place. Doors OF ',RUNCORN ONNTLFMAN IN New The sudden death of Mr. William Rigby, late of Runcorn, which took place at his residence, Moodat St. John, Rem- eerie, on Wednesday night, the 291 h Sept., is announced.. The deceased left Runcorn in the spring of the present year for Remuera, where he arrived on the 22n0l June last. Up to the day before lointleath he enjoyed go,' health, when he complained of being troubled with a bad cold, and passed a sleepless night. According to his mual custom lie got up early on Wednesday morning, hut was unable to resume his customary work, and had to return to bed. A doctor was sent for. Meanwhile the deceased became unconscious, sod never recovered consciousness. After living for about 12 hours in this elate he expired. Mr. Rigby was 49 years of age, and was accompanied to the colony by his wife, three daughter. and aeon-in-law (Mr. Pearson). The decemed I woe for many years a ship-broker in Runcorn, and at one time carried ou an extensive business. During his short residence in Auckland he made many friends, and being a prominent and enthusiastic Freemason he took an active part in the furtherance of the welfare of the craft. Before his departure frotn England he had gained the dignity of Past Provincial Grand Pursuivant of the Grand Lodge of Cheshire. In 1854 tote. Rigby was elected a member of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, which post he retained fur 14 years. He wae very closely connected with the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company, and rendered valuable service to this company daring his asso- ciation with it, and when he left England he took with him the good opinion of thedirectors and shareholders. For many years he was one of the overseer, for the township of Run- corn, and fulfill.' the duties of the office to the satisfaction of everyone concerned.

LRCTCRR OW "SCISSORS TO GRIM," AT WIDIALS.—The Rev. J. Tessyman, of Widnes, delivered a lecture, entitled Sciosors to Grind," in Tracey-street Wesleyan Methodist Bchmbroom, on Tuesday evening, in aid of the circuit funds. Mr. Benjamin Brown presided, and there was. good attendance. The Lecturer first referred to the honour con- ferred on Columbus, the discoverer of America, and add he had never heard of the man who invented SCISSWA, whoever he might be, having been crowned with the laurel wreath. It would have been quite possible for the world to have done without such a famous invention as that of the electric telegraph, but how could we have done with- out scissors? Captain Cook was rewarded with a gold medal for sailing round the globe, and poets and philosophers bad their statues, but he should like to know how the services rendered by these men could compare with the usefulness of scissors. He found that poets had written on almost everything, but it WAS provoking to find that nobody had sung of the glories of scissors. (Laughter.) An American had composed a poelis cal effusion addressed to buckets, but not a soul appeared to have unburdened himself concerning the useful article on which he had to speak that evening_ This, however, was only another illustration of the saying that true worth was often neglected. It would hardly he too much to say that modern civilised life was. in II great measure built up on the foundation of scissors. What would a barber do without scissors? (Great laughter). By this instrument they were enabled to maintain themselves in a sort of decency. Mr. Tessyrnan then instanced a nom- bar of ways in which bcissors were useful in domestic life. lie had often wondered how any one got rich by grioding these useful instruments. They had heard of sweeps rising to be mayors of London, but no such good fortune had fallen to the grinder of scissors, who was a useful citizen in his way, which could not be said of every British workman. In conclusion, the speaker referral to various lessons lobe learnt from scissors. The first was that they were sharper after grinding, and so some folks were sharper after trial and isisfortune they bad a better appearance alter grinding, and this was how character ought to be I they were willing workers, and so should men be : scissors did not lals,ot for their own, but for the benefit of Whets ; scimori worked better alter being sharpened, and so did men after ! discipline. A vote f thanks was peered to the lecturer, on the motion of Mr. Robinson, seconded hr Mr. Sadler, and ! supported by the Rev. C. Bingen'.

HELENS PkiILTAMENTIART DIMATINO SOCIETY.— H e Onstinvan.—On Friday night the benches of the Roam were well filled with members, many also having to stand, a fact ehowing that the interest in the proceedinge of the Rouse has not abated. The stranger's gallery, front which the spectators have • bird's eye view of the mock statute makers, was well tilled with an attentive body of onlookers who take a lively interest in the debate, and show their an- , preciation of a "gird hit," by 'lmp shrugsof the shoulders, and suggeetive facial contortions ; the cheering which for- merly emanated from this part of the House having been put down by the. Speaker. Jr is, however, very difficult to suppress the exhibition of feeling in entliusiaffiic pffiticians, and, on a late occasion, the member for Warwickehire with an expression of the utmost ctincern on big aristocratic physiognomy, drew the attention of the Speaker to the fact that the strangera in the watery were taking part in the ancient custOm—but very laughable one in our Parliament— of taking the feeling of the House by shouts of "Ave," and No," on questions before the HOEV. The strangers again, of course, were counselled, to refrain from ebullitions of I feeling, and from taking part in the proceedingn of l'arlia- ment. The debate on the Irish Dieturhance Bill was re- maned on Friday night by the member for Woodstock (Conservative), who made a good speech for his party ; !it was deliverel in an eloquent manner. The Secretary for the Colonies followed, and made fun of Con- servative sympathy for Irish distress. and asked how it was no measure for the alleviation of Irish mieery was intro- duced by the Conservatives, and no attempt roade to check the growth of the distress. The member for Westminster eupported the amendment that the bill he read that day six ' months, and the third member for the City of ttlargew remarked that it wee time they legislated fnt the tenant. as for the last hundred years they hail been legislating for the landlord. The member for Gloaceeter supported the amend- ment, and the member for Bath, who rose front the I-iberal side, gave another of his impassioned speeches, the perora- tion being no lege humornusthan it was vigorous in style. The Leader of the Opposition, who has shown himself to be an ' assiduous and earnest member. reviesrel calmly the essen- , tial points in the bill, and was followed by the Secretary for Ireland, who cleverly dealt with the objections to the menetire fnim the Opposition Ride. A division was taken, and tbe bill was passed bat a maiority of two.—The Leader of the Opposition at the next meeting will introduce a , measure dealing with the Eastern Question.

LEFTWICH EIVIWIITAINWEITT.—An entertainment in con- nection with the Temperance movement in Leftwich was given on Saturday evening. .Mr. George Slater, of Witton Lodge, presided. There was a large attendance. Songs. readings, and recitations were given bv Mr. Howarth, Mr. and Mrs Pierce, Mile Alcock, and Mr. Dutton and the Union children. The proceedings passed off very pleasantly NU WTHWICH EVIDENTLY Nelms LOOILINg Anus.— We were recently at Morthwich, whore the chief trade in pumping brine out of the ground in order to produce com- mon salt, and were much astonished by the appearance pre- sented by part of it. The effect cf continued pumping ' causes the surface of the ground to sink, and this subsidence results in wrions damage to building property. end 'not bei:;re it was . It would be difficult by words to convey an idea of the sad condition of many part. of the town. Or, have they come to the conclusion that t. deodorirers these things are utterly worthlere, but as mete eatleta for foul gaeesand diseam they are useful or, is it that having tried a argent and found it damped with failure they are disgusted, have lust heart or grown careless r Whether they new the matter in the seri.. light in which they might to do or not, some of their number became quite sereouely prostrated, and for the moment terribly alarmal whenever the diseases which the present state of things pro- duce happen to develop thetnselves within 100 yards of their own homes, and soon raise to outcry against effects eagenderel by their own negligence and original blundering, yet never not try to remove the mischirf creator—tbe first

MI through the collapse of a Tay Bridge scores cf our fellow beings are in a moment put out of existence, tbe horror of nil is manifest, and a ...arching inqulty is de- nneadeu to prevent similar otteurrences in future, and Ming home to the proper parties the cause of the disaster. But when an insidious disease is stealthily removing a few here and a few there, no more than a memenLtry notice is taken of it, and no action or remedy it, although in the aggregate the victims of the latter should for exceed that of the former.

It may not be this year, it may not be next, but that the time will certainly come I have not the slightest doubt, when thia system will not be allowed, and tenet be altered, but I fear, jad,ing from past experience, unless the matter be presenttal before some higher authority than our local one, it will not be done until many.more veined and neeful linen have been sacrificed to such apathy and negligence. Another idea connected with this matter is, that as inter- ments increase the disease germs increase, and as these latter inmaters no will the suffering and death, and as the variation of level in this diatrict is conaiderable, the greatest danger will lie Cl the highest points, or upper portions of the dis- trict, the very points at WiliCil there has been already the greatest atnount of sickness and death. Who then among our representatives will come forward, and throwing aside all parsisnonioutmeas seek to abate one of the moat grows and most deadly nuieances of modern times, thus lessening the possibility and probability of our fellow townsmen suffering months el sickness or being carried away by diseases, and nervously prostrating others who have not the courege of their convictions. TOI3IAS TENBY. Runcorn, November 23, 1890.

A young person between 12 and HI sent too reformatory to be still previously sent to prison for not lees than ten dam beta° removal to the reformatory. O. That section. 10 and 11 of the Summon' Jurisdiction Act, 1879, should be extended to non-indictable offences, and that the age under which whipping may he inflicted he extended from 14 to 18. 7. That no young person between 12 and 16 thould be mat to primon • second time without also being sent (Os reformatory. 8. That some portion of the coat of the maintenance of the inmates of reformatory and industrial schvols should be paid out of the funds of the poor-law union to which the parentsare or would be chargeable if receiving relief the guardians having power to recover the money front the persons legally liable for the maintenance of such inmates. 9. That it is expedient, if possible, that some provision !should be made for greater certainty as to the reception in reformatory and industrial schools of juveniles sent to them by the magistrate.— The Deputy Chairman explained that the leading principles of these resolutions was that there should be no imprison- ment under twelve except undor exceptional cireumstancen; and colt, to cause greater responsibility to attach to parents 411 juiadredaiaz (tom tdlore,,gwt cwoint the ofe p,?l d einrinaev mnp. rioAnn moot before sending a child to a reformatory: but the mana- gers of these institutions had felt. st.ngly to these points, and inade such tdrong representations that they alwaye held tth the fact to the children under their care that they had already been punished, as a strong motive for their refo tion, that the magistrates' committee had recommended the , retentien of that provision, although the general public hart, herein favour of its abolition. The chairman of the com- mittee (Lord Tollemache) had sent a letter saying that on consideration he thought whipping should not be twactised on youth. over 14, while the committee recommended that the section of the act which provided fry the whipping of children for indictable offence from 10 lb 14 years of age nhoutd he extended to non-indictable offences, euch as stone throwing and window breaking, and alto to offenders up to 18 years of age. lie proposed that the resolutions he printed and Bent to every magistrate in the county, with the regent that they be considered between now and the January ses- sions, when they would 1,, finally discussed.—The Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P., eecontled, and added that a note shofld be appended to the resolution as to whipping to the effect that Lord Tollemache would move that it be not ex- tended beyond 14 years of ago.—The resolution was then adopted.

Nlajor-General Hutchinson, RE., hae reported to the Board of Trade the result of his inquiry into the circumstances connected with the collision which occurred on the 29th ult. near St. Ilelens Junction Station, on the London and North-Western Railway. During o dense fog the 12 o'clock midnight down passenger train front London for Liverpool, due to pass St. Helans Junction signal cabin at about six a.m., came into collision with an unattached engine and tender which had been standing on the moiu down line waiting to set hack into a siding. Three paasengers one stated to have been slightly injured, and the driver of the passenger train hod hie hack hurt. Major-tieneral Hutchin- son finds that this accident was the result of a breach a rules and of an act of forgetfulness on the port of the signal- man on duty in St. Ilelens Junction signal cabin, who had just completed 12 !lowa' night duty, and had probably falkn into a doze. It is highly probable," Major-General Hutchinson adds, that this collision would have been alto- gether prevented, or its effects, at any rate, greatly miti- gated, had the express train been provided with a larger amount of brake power, instontaneously applicable by the driver. The occurrence of this collivion, owing to the for- getfulness of a signalman at the end of 12 hours' night duty (which, by a private arrangement between the men, seems to have been prolonged,. a rule, to nearly 13 brain.), raises up the important question whether in those posts where the nature or inqw,rtence of the work does rot justify the employment of more than two men in the 21 hones, it is wise to make the night duty of ouch long duration as 12 hours.
